question: Why do you want to study Sports Coaching?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific motivation grounded in real experience with coaching, not just a love of playing sport.

bullets: Distinguish wanting to coach from simply wanting to play or watch sport
Point to a concrete moment or experience that sparked the interest
Show you understand coaching is about developing other people, not just yourself
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've played football competitively since I was seven, but what actually pulled me toward coaching was helping run my club's under-10s sessions last year. I loved playing, but I realised I got even more satisfaction watching a kid finally land a skill they'd been struggling with for weeks. That shift, from wanting to perform myself to wanting to build that moment for someone else, is what made me sure coaching was the direction I wanted to study.

commonMistakes: Answering as if the question was 'why do you love sport'
No real coaching exposure to back the claim
Sounding like a backup plan for not making it as a player
followUps: What's the difference between being a great player and being a great coach?

question: Why did you choose our Sports Coaching course specifically, rather than a general Sports Science degree elsewhere?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into the course structure, placements, or staff, showing this choice is deliberate rather than generic.

bullets: Name a specific feature of the course such as a placement scheme, a module, or coaching qualifications built in
Explain why that feature matters to your own goals
Show you understand how this differs from a broader sports science route
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked at a few sports science courses, but yours is one of the only ones that gets you out coaching in schools and clubs from first year rather than saving all the practical work for a placement year at the end. I want to be tested on my delivery early and get that feedback loop going as soon as possible. I also read that the course builds in national governing body coaching awards alongside the degree, which means I'd leave with something I can actually use on a CV straight away, not just theory.

commonMistakes: Praise that could apply to any sports course
Citing rankings or reputation alone
Confusing coaching-focused content with a pure sports science syllabus
followUps: Which module on the course are you most looking forward to, and why?

question: Tell us about your own background in sport and how it led you here.
lookingFor: A coherent personal story connecting playing or participation history to the decision to coach.

bullets: Give a brief honest account of your own sporting background
Identify the turning point that shifted you toward coaching
Connect it clearly to why you're applying now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I swam competitively through school but was never going to be elite, and I made peace with that around sixteen. What kept me in the pool was my club's junior swim teacher asking me to help time and encourage the younger kids at training, and I found I genuinely looked forward to those sessions more than my own. That experience, watching someone go from scared of the deep end to swimming a length unaided, is what convinced me coaching was the path I actually wanted, not just staying involved in swimming.

commonMistakes: Treating the question as purely about personal athletic achievement
No clear link between the sporting history and the decision to coach
Overstating athletic credentials that don't hold up under follow-up
followUps: What did that junior swim teacher do well that you'd want to copy?

question: What coaching or leadership experience have you had so far, and what did you learn from it?
lookingFor: Concrete, specific experience with genuine reflection on what it taught them, not a resume list.

bullets: Describe one specific role, session, or team rather than listing everything
Explain a real challenge you faced in that role
State what you learned or changed as a result
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For the past year I've been an assistant coach with my old netball club's under-14 team, running warm-ups and small-sided drills under the head coach. Early on I planned every session down to the minute and got thrown when half the group finished a drill faster than expected, so I've learned to build in extension activities and read the room rather than sticking rigidly to a plan. It taught me that a session plan is a starting point, not a script, and that being able to adapt on the spot matters more than I first assumed.

commonMistakes: Listing multiple roles with no depth on any of them
No genuine challenge or learning mentioned
Taking full credit for a team's results as if solely responsible
followUps: How did the head coach's feedback on that change your approach afterward?

question: Have you read anything about coaching outside your own experience that's shaped how you think about it?
lookingFor: Evidence of genuine independent engagement with coaching ideas, with the ability to explain why it mattered, not just name-drop a title.

bullets: Name a specific book, article, podcast, or course that goes beyond personal experience
Explain one concrete idea from it in your own words
Show how it actually changed or challenged your thinking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read The Talent Code by Daniel Coyle after a teacher recommended it, and the idea that stuck with me was deep practice, that skill grows fastest from struggling right at the edge of your ability rather than from repeating things you've already mastered. It made me rethink how I ran drills with the under-14s I help coach, because I'd been making sessions comfortable rather than deliberately hard. I started building in drills just above their current level, and I noticed they engaged more, not less, even though it was harder.

commonMistakes: Naming a title with no understanding of its actual content
Only citing personal playing experience when asked about wider reading
An idea that sounds memorised rather than genuinely absorbed
followUps: Did you disagree with anything in it?

question: Who is a coach, at any level, that you admire, and why?
lookingFor: A specific, thought-through answer that reveals genuine coaching values, not just a famous name.

bullets: Pick someone you can speak about with real detail, famous or not
Identify a specific quality or method, not just their trophies
Connect it to your own coaching philosophy
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It's actually my own school PE teacher, Mr. Adeyemi, more than any famous name. What I admired was how differently he treated each of us. He knew that I needed pushing hard while a quieter teammate needed encouragement before criticism, and he adjusted on the fly without ever making it feel unfair. That's the part of coaching I find most interesting, not the tactics but reading individual people, and it's exactly what I want to get better at studying this course.

commonMistakes: Naming a famous coach purely for their win record
No specific quality identified beyond 'they're successful'
An answer disconnected from the applicant's own values
followUps: Is there anything about their approach you'd do differently?

question: What do you understand by the term Long-Term Athlete Development, and why does it matter?
lookingFor: A basic grasp of age-appropriate development stages and the reasoning behind avoiding early specialisation.

bullets: Explain that LTAD is a framework of stages matching training to a young athlete's physical and mental maturity, not just age
Mention the risk of pushing performance too early, such as burnout or injury
Give a practical example of what it looks like in a session
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Long-Term Athlete Development is the idea that what you ask of a young athlete should match their stage of physical and mental maturity rather than just their age, so a coach builds broad movement skills and enjoyment first before layering on structured training and competition. The reasoning is that pushing intense specialisation too early raises the risk of burnout, overuse injury, and kids dropping out of sport altogether. In practice that means an under-9s session I've helped run focuses on varied games and coordination rather than drilling one sport's technique for an hour.

commonMistakes: Treating LTAD as simply 'train harder as you get older'
No mention of the risks of early specialisation
A definition with no practical example
followUps: What would you say to a parent who wants their eight-year-old specialising in one sport now?

question: What's the difference between coaching someone and simply teaching them a technique?
lookingFor: Understanding that coaching involves ongoing relationship, motivation, and adapting to the individual, beyond instructing a skill once.

bullets: Note that teaching a technique can be a single transfer of information
Explain coaching as an ongoing relationship involving motivation, feedback, and adapting over time
Give an example showing the difference in practice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Teaching a technique can happen in a single instruction, like showing someone the correct grip on a racket. Coaching is what happens after that, going back to it session after session, working out why they keep reverting to the old grip under pressure, and adjusting how you explain it until it actually sticks for that specific person. It's really about building a relationship over time, not just transferring information once, which is why the same technical correction can look completely different depending on who you're coaching.

commonMistakes: Treating the two terms as identical
No mention of the relational or ongoing element of coaching
An answer with no concrete example
followUps: Can you think of a time a purely technical correction didn't work, and what you did instead?

question: What's the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic motivation, and which do you think a coach should try to build in an athlete?
lookingFor: A clear grasp of the two concepts plus a reasoned, not one-sided, view on their role in coaching.

bullets: Define intrinsic motivation as doing something for its own enjoyment and extrinsic as doing it for an external reward
Argue that intrinsic motivation tends to sustain effort longer, especially through setbacks
Acknowledge that extrinsic rewards like medals or praise still have a place, especially with younger athletes
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Intrinsic motivation is doing something because you genuinely enjoy it or find it satisfying, while extrinsic motivation is doing it for an outside reward like a trophy, praise, or making a team. From what I've read and seen coaching younger athletes, intrinsic motivation tends to be what keeps people going through a bad run of form, because the reward doesn't depend on results. That said, I don't think extrinsic motivators are bad, especially with children, since a bit of praise or a small reward can hook someone in before the intrinsic love of the sport has had a chance to develop.

commonMistakes: Reversing the two definitions
Dismissing extrinsic motivation as always harmful
No connection to actual coaching practice
followUps: How would you try to build intrinsic motivation in a young athlete who's only there because their parents signed them up?

question: What do you understand by a growth mindset, and how might a coach encourage one?
lookingFor: Basic understanding of the concept plus a practical, coaching-specific application, not just a dictionary definition.

bullets: Explain growth mindset as the belief that ability can improve through effort, as opposed to fixed talent
Contrast it briefly with a fixed mindset
Give a concrete coaching behaviour that encourages it, such as praising effort and process over natural ability
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A growth mindset is the belief that ability isn't fixed, it can be built through practice and effort, whereas a fixed mindset assumes you're either naturally good at something or you're not. As a coach I think the way you give feedback matters a lot here, praising the process, like the extra hours someone put into fixing their backhand, rather than just saying 'you're a natural.' I try to do that with the kids I help coach, focusing comments on what they worked on rather than just whether they won.

commonMistakes: A vague or buzzword-only definition with no application
Confusing growth mindset with simple positivity
No mention of how feedback language reinforces it
followUps: What would you say to a player who says 'I'm just not talented enough' after a loss?

question: In simple terms, what is periodization, and why do coaches use it?
lookingFor: A basic but accurate grasp of structuring training over time to peak for competition and avoid overtraining.

bullets: Describe periodization as planning training in phases across a season rather than training the same way every week
Mention the goal of peaking for key competitions while managing fatigue and injury risk
Note it usually involves varying intensity and volume over time
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Periodization is planning an athlete's training in structured phases across a season rather than doing the same intensity of session every week. You might build a base of general fitness early on, then shift toward more sport-specific and higher-intensity work as a key competition approaches, then taper down just before it so the athlete is fresh rather than fatigued. The point is to manage the balance between building fitness and avoiding overtraining or injury, so performance actually peaks when it matters.

commonMistakes: Describing periodization as simply 'training hard all the time'
No mention of peaking for competition or tapering
An answer with no sense of phases across a season
followUps: What might go wrong if a coach ignored periodization altogether?

question: How would you run a single session for a group with a wide range of ability levels?
lookingFor: Practical understanding of differentiation, such as adjusting task difficulty, grouping, or constraints rather than running one fixed drill for everyone.

bullets: Recognise the core problem: one drill at one difficulty will bore some and overwhelm others
Suggest a concrete method, such as adjustable constraints, grouping by ability, or offering task variations
Mention keeping the group together socially even while differentiating the challenge
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd try to keep everyone doing broadly the same activity so no one feels singled out, but build in ways to change the difficulty within it, like widening or narrowing a target area, or letting stronger players add a second touch restriction while others get more time on the ball. I've done this helping run mixed-ability sessions, where I'd quietly adjust the distance or the rules for a pair struggling and make it harder for a pair cruising through it. It keeps the whole group moving together while still challenging each person at roughly the right level.

commonMistakes: Proposing to simply split the group and ignore the weaker players
No concrete method for adjusting difficulty
Assuming one drill fits everyone equally
followUps: How would you handle a parent who complains their advanced child isn't being challenged enough?

question: Why is safeguarding such an important part of coaching, especially with young athletes?
lookingFor: Awareness that coaches hold a position of trust and responsibility, with some sense of what safeguarding covers in practice.

bullets: Explain that coaches are in a position of trust and authority over children or vulnerable athletes
Mention that safeguarding covers physical, emotional, and welfare concerns, not just obvious abuse
Show awareness that coaches have a duty to notice, report, and follow proper procedures rather than handle concerns informally
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A coach ends up in a position of real trust and authority over young athletes, often spending more one-on-one time with them than most adults outside their family, so that trust has to come with real responsibility. Safeguarding isn't just about preventing obvious abuse, it also covers things like noticing if a young athlete seems anxious, withdrawn, or is being pushed too hard by a parent, and knowing it's not my place to investigate that myself but to follow the club's proper reporting procedure. I think a good coach treats that responsibility as seriously as any tactical or technical part of the job.

commonMistakes: Reducing safeguarding to only physical abuse
Suggesting they would handle a serious concern informally themselves
No acknowledgment of the coach's position of trust
followUps: What would you do if a young athlete told you something concerning in confidence?

question: What do you know about how sport currently handles concussion, and why has it become such a significant issue?
lookingFor: Awareness of current concussion protocols and the shift toward athlete welfare over playing through injury, with some grasp of the reasoning.

bullets: Mention the 'if in doubt, sit them out' principle and graduated return-to-play protocols
Note the growing evidence linking repeated head injury to long-term harm, which is why the issue has gained attention
Show understanding that this shifts responsibility onto coaches to prioritise welfare over short-term performance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There's been a real shift in sports like rugby and football toward taking any suspected head knock seriously, with the principle being if in doubt, sit them out, followed by a graduated return-to-play process rather than letting someone back on immediately if they seem fine. It's become such a major issue because of growing research linking repeated concussions to long-term conditions, which has pushed governing bodies to introduce mandatory protocols and stricter rules on contact in training. As a coach I think that means resisting any pressure, even from the athlete themselves, to rush someone back before they're properly cleared.

commonMistakes: Suggesting a player can be judged fit to continue based on how they look
No awareness of graduated return-to-play protocols
Treating it as a minor or outdated concern
followUps: What would you do if a talented player insisted they felt fine minutes after a head knock?

question: How would you adapt a session to include an athlete with a physical disability?
lookingFor: Practical thinking about adapting equipment, rules, or tasks so the athlete is genuinely included rather than sidelined, plus awareness of asking rather than assuming.

bullets: Emphasise talking to the athlete first about what they need rather than assuming
Suggest concrete adaptations such as modified equipment, rules, or classifications used in adapted sport
Aim to keep the athlete genuinely part of the group activity, not just present but sidelined
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The first thing I'd do is actually ask the athlete, or their parent if they're young, what adaptations work for them, rather than guessing what I think they need. Depending on the sport that might mean adjusting equipment, like a lighter or larger ball, changing a rule such as allowing an extra bounce, or restructuring a drill so it doesn't depend on the specific movement they can't do. What matters most to me is that the adaptation lets them genuinely compete and contribute within the session, not just stand on the sideline with a watered-down version of the activity.

commonMistakes: Assuming what the athlete needs without asking them
An adaptation that effectively excludes the athlete from the main activity
Treating inclusion as a one-off accommodation rather than an ongoing conversation
followUps: Have you seen or heard of a specific adapted sport format, like wheelchair basketball's rules?

question: What's the difference between an autocratic and a democratic coaching style, and when might each be appropriate?
lookingFor: Clear grasp of the two styles plus contextual judgement about when each fits, rather than declaring one universally correct.

bullets: Define autocratic as coach-led, giving direct instructions, and democratic as involving athletes in decisions
Give an example situation where autocratic suits better, such as a safety-critical or time-pressured moment
Give an example where democratic suits better, such as building ownership with experienced athletes
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An autocratic style is where the coach makes the decisions and gives direct instructions, while a democratic style involves the athletes in working out the plan together. I think autocratic makes sense in situations where there's a safety issue or very little time, like calling a specific play in the last minute of a match. But for something like planning a training week with older, more experienced athletes, a more democratic approach tends to build buy-in and actually teaches them to think for themselves, which matters more the longer term you're coaching someone.

commonMistakes: Claiming one style is always correct in every situation
Mixing up the two definitions
No situational reasoning for when each applies
followUps: Which style is closer to your own natural instinct, and why?

question: How would you give feedback to an athlete who's just performed badly, without knocking their confidence?
lookingFor: Understanding of constructive, specific feedback rather than vague praise or blunt criticism, showing awareness of tone and timing.

bullets: Mention being specific rather than vague, pointing to one or two concrete things to work on
Balance honesty about what went wrong with recognition of effort or something that went right
Consider timing, such as giving space to cool down before a detailed conversation
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd try not to pile everything on at once, so I'd pick one or two specific, fixable things rather than a long list of what went wrong. I'd also want to name something that did go right, even something small like their positioning being good, so it's honest rather than just softened criticism. And I'd think about timing, giving them a bit of space to cool down right after a bad performance rather than launching into feedback the second they come off, because people take in criticism better once the immediate disappointment has settled.

commonMistakes: Only offering vague, generic praise with no substance
A long list of every mistake delivered at once
Ignoring the timing and emotional state of the athlete
followUps: What if the athlete gets defensive when you raise it?

question: One athlete in your squad is talented but consistently disrupts sessions and undermines your instructions in front of the group. How would you handle it?
lookingFor: Structured, mature thinking that balances fairness to the group with a private, respectful approach to the individual, rather than a snap punitive reaction.

bullets: Address the group disruption calmly in the moment without escalating publicly
Follow up with a private conversation to understand what's driving the behaviour
Set clear, consistent expectations while keeping the door open for the athlete to improve
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: In the moment I'd keep my response calm and brief, redirecting the group back to the task rather than getting into a public standoff that gives the behaviour an audience. Afterward I'd speak to the athlete privately, not to tell them off straight away but to actually understand what's behind it, whether it's boredom, something going on outside the sport, or feeling unchallenged given their talent. From there I'd set clear expectations about what's acceptable going forward, and make clear that talent doesn't exempt them from the same standards as everyone else, while still leaving room for them to turn it around.

commonMistakes: Publicly confronting or humiliating the athlete in front of the group
Ignoring the behaviour because the athlete is talented
No attempt to understand the underlying cause
followUps: What if a private conversation doesn't change anything?

question: What are the risks of trying to identify talented young athletes too early?
lookingFor: Awareness that early talent identification is unreliable and can be harmful, including late developers being missed and pressure on selected athletes.

bullets: Mention the relative age effect and that physical maturity at a young age is a poor predictor of long-term ability
Note the risk of talented late developers being overlooked and dropping out
Raise the psychological pressure placed on children labelled 'talented' too soon
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The biggest risk is that early physical maturity often gets mistaken for talent, which is part of what's called the relative age effect, where kids born earlier in the school year tend to be picked more often simply because they're bigger and stronger at that point, not necessarily more skilled long term. That means genuinely talented but smaller or later-developing kids can get overlooked and drop out before they ever catch up physically. There's also a real psychological cost to labelling a child 'talented' too early, since it can create pressure that actually works against their development rather than helping it.

commonMistakes: Assuming early physical dominance reliably predicts future ability
No mention of the relative age effect or late developers
Treating early identification as purely positive with no downside
followUps: How might a coach design a program to reduce this bias?

question: How might a coach help build confidence in an athlete who's talented but consistently doubts themselves under pressure?
lookingFor: Some grasp of practical sports psychology tools like process goals, controlled exposure to pressure, or reframing self-talk, rather than generic encouragement.

bullets: Suggest setting process or performance goals rather than purely outcome goals, so success isn't only judged by winning
Mention building pressure gradually in training so competition doesn't feel unfamiliar
Note the value of helping the athlete notice and reframe negative self-talk
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd try shifting their goals away from pure outcomes like winning, toward process goals they can actually control, like executing a specific technique well, so their sense of success isn't only tied to the scoreboard. I'd also want to build pressure into training deliberately, like simulating a close-match scenario, so competition pressure feels familiar rather than overwhelming the first time it matters. And I'd try to get them noticing their own self-talk, because a lot of doubt shows up as an internal running commentary, and just becoming aware of it is often the first step to changing it.

commonMistakes: Relying purely on generic encouragement like 'believe in yourself'
Focusing only on outcome goals such as winning
No mention of practicing under simulated pressure
followUps: Have you ever had to manage your own nerves before a big performance, and what did you do?

question: What do you understand by the term physical literacy, and why does it matter in youth coaching?
lookingFor: Understanding of physical literacy as broad fundamental movement competence and confidence, and its role as a foundation before sport-specific skill.

bullets: Define physical literacy as the fundamental movement skills, confidence, and motivation to be active across a range of activities
Distinguish it from sport-specific technical skill
Explain why it matters as a foundation for later specialisation and lifelong activity
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Physical literacy is the broad foundation of movement, things like running, jumping, throwing, and balance, along with the confidence and motivation to keep being active, rather than skill in one specific sport. I think it matters hugely in youth coaching because a child with strong physical literacy can pick up almost any sport more easily later on, whereas one who's only ever practised a single sport's specific technique often struggles when the demands change. It's also just as much about building a lasting love of movement, so kids stay active well beyond their competitive years.

commonMistakes: Confusing physical literacy with sport-specific technique
No mention of the confidence or motivation aspect
Treating it as only relevant to elite pathways
followUps: What kind of activities would you use with a group of six-year-olds to build physical literacy?

question: What role do you think technology like video analysis or GPS tracking should play in coaching?
lookingFor: A balanced view that technology is a useful tool for feedback and workload management, without overstating it as a replacement for coaching judgement.

bullets: Give a concrete example such as video analysis for technique or GPS for monitoring training load
Explain the benefit, such as objective evidence or catching things the eye misses
Note the limits, that data still needs a coach's judgement and human context to interpret
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think video analysis is really valuable because it lets an athlete actually see what a coach is describing, like watching their own foot position on a serve rather than just hearing about it, which can make a correction click much faster. GPS and load-tracking tools are useful too, for spotting when an athlete's training load is creeping up in a way that raises injury risk before it becomes obvious. But I don't think any of that replaces coaching judgement, the numbers still need someone who knows the athlete to interpret what they actually mean and decide what to do about it.

commonMistakes: Dismissing technology as unnecessary or a gimmick
Suggesting data alone can replace coaching judgement
No concrete example of an actual tool or use case
followUps: Can you think of a downside to relying too heavily on data-driven coaching?

question: An athlete you coach asks you about supplements that are close to the line of what's permitted. How would you respond?
lookingFor: Clear ethical reasoning that prioritises the athlete's health and the integrity of the sport over short-term performance gains, without being preachy or naive.

bullets: State clearly that you would not encourage or help source anything near a banned substance
Explain the reasoning: health risk, fairness, and the athlete's long-term reputation and eligibility
Offer a constructive alternative, such as directing them to legitimate nutrition or performance advice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd be honest with them that I wouldn't help them go anywhere near that line, and I'd explain why rather than just saying no. Beyond the obvious risk of a ban, there are real health risks with under-regulated supplements, and testing doesn't always catch contamination until it's already cost someone their career. I'd rather redirect that conversation toward what legitimate nutrition and recovery changes could actually improve their performance, because in my experience most athletes asking that question are really just looking for any edge, and there's usually a safer one available if we look properly.

commonMistakes: Being vague or evasive instead of giving a clear answer
Lecturing without offering any constructive alternative
Underestimating the health risks involved
followUps: What would you do if you suspected an athlete was already doping?

question: What are some basic things a coach can do to reduce the risk of injury in training?
lookingFor: Practical, sensible awareness such as proper warm-ups, gradual load progression, and listening to athlete-reported pain, not just generic caution.

bullets: Mention a structured warm-up that prepares the body for the session ahead
Note the importance of not increasing training load too quickly
Emphasise taking athlete-reported pain or fatigue seriously rather than pushing through it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A proper warm-up matters a lot, not just jogging a lap but actually raising heart rate and mobilising the joints that are about to be used heavily. I'd also try not to increase training intensity or volume too sharply from one week to the next, since sudden jumps in load are a common cause of overuse injuries. And practically, if an athlete tells me something feels off, even something small, I'd take that seriously rather than assuming they're just being cautious, because catching a niggle early is a lot better than dealing with a full injury later.

commonMistakes: Treating warm-up as a box to tick rather than genuinely preparing the body
Ignoring gradual load progression
Dismissing an athlete's reported pain to keep a session on schedule
followUps: How would you handle an athlete who wants to push through pain to stay in a big game?

question: Where do you see your coaching career heading after this course, and how does the degree fit into that?
lookingFor: A grounded, realistic direction connected clearly to what the course offers, showing some awareness of the range of paths available in coaching.

bullets: Give a genuine direction, whether grassroots, school sport, performance pathway, or another route, without over-claiming certainty
Show awareness that coaching careers often build gradually through qualifications and experience
Connect the specific things the course offers to that direction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I'm most drawn to working in athlete development at a school or academy level, helping young players build a foundation before they specialise, rather than aiming straight for elite performance coaching. I know that path usually means building up national governing body qualifications and practical hours alongside a degree, which is exactly why this course's built-in placements and coaching awards appeal to me, they let me start accumulating that real experience while I study rather than afterward. I'm open to the specifics changing as I learn more, but that's the direction I want to head in.

commonMistakes: An unrealistically specific plan with no room for growth
A goal completely disconnected from what the course actually offers
Vague ambition with no direction at all, such as just 'working in sport'
followUps: What's the first coaching qualification or experience you'd want to pursue after this degree?
